title: Put the wrong fuel in
h1: I put the wrong fuel in my car. What do I do?
metaDesc: Put diesel in a gas car, gas in a diesel, or the wrong octane? See whether to start the engine, how urgent it is, and what a shop will do.
synonyms: put diesel in my gas car
put diesel in car by mistake
filled up with the wrong fuel
car running bad after getting gas
intro: Putting the wrong fuel in is a common mistake, and what to do next depends on which fuel went in and whether you've started the engine. Diesel in a gas car, or gas in a diesel, can badly damage the engine if you run it. A lower octane than your car calls for is usually much less serious.
safety: If you put diesel in a gas car or gas in a diesel, don't start the engine. If you haven't turned the key or pressed Start yet, leave it off.
If fuel spilled on you, the car or the ground, keep away from sparks and flames, and don't smoke.
If the car sputters, smokes or loses power after filling up, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.

q_what.help: Your receipt usually shows the fuel type and grade. Your fuel door, gas cap or owner's manual shows what your car needs.

opts.a: Gasoline in a diesel car or truck
Regular (lower octane) in a car that needs premium
Premium in a car that only needs regular
E85 or 'Flex Fuel' in a car that isn't flex-fuel
I'm not sure what went in

q_diesel_started.q: Has the engine been started since you filled up?

opts.a: Yes, I started it or drove it

q_gas_started.q: Has the engine been started since you filled up?

opts.a: Yes, I started it or drove it

result.title: Diesel in a gas car: don't start it. The tank needs to be drained
result.now: Don't start the engine. Tell the station staff, then have the car towed to a shop that can drain the fuel tank. If it has to be moved away from the pump, push it with help instead of starting it.
if: If you only added a little before you noticed, still don't start it. Let the shop decide whether draining is needed.
Keep your receipt. It shows what was pumped and how much.
result.why: Gas engines can't burn diesel properly. Diesel is thick and oily, so it can clog the fuel system and foul the spark plugs. Ford's advice is not to start the engine at all with the wrong fuel in the tank. If the engine hasn't run, the fix is usually draining the tank and refilling with the right fuel.

causes.clues: Your receipt or the pump says diesel.

causes.name: Diesel already in the fuel lines
causes.clues: The key was turned to ON, which can run the fuel pump for a moment.

you: Check your receipt for the fuel type and amount.
shop: Drain the fuel tank
Flush the fuel lines
Refill with the correct fuel

result.title: Diesel in a gas car after starting: turn it off and have it towed
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn off the engine and don't restart it. Have the car towed to a shop that can drain and flush the fuel system.
if: If the check engine light is flashing or there's thick smoke from the exhaust, tell the shop. The catalytic converter in the exhaust may need to be checked.
If you smell fuel or see a leak, keep away from sparks and flames.
result.why: Once diesel reaches the engine, it doesn't burn cleanly. That causes heavy smoke, misfires and stalling, and it can damage the catalytic converter. The less the engine runs on it, the less damage it's likely to do.

causes.name: Diesel in the tank and fuel lines
causes.clues: The engine ran rough, smoked or stalled soon after filling up.

causes.name: Fouled spark plugs
causes.clues: The engine misfires or won't restart.

causes.name: Overheated catalytic converter
causes.clues: A flashing check engine light, or a hot, burning smell from under the car.

you: Keep your receipt and note how far the car went after filling up.
shop: Drain the tank and flush the fuel lines
Replace the fuel filter if the car has one
Check the spark plugs and catalytic converter
Code scan

result.title: Gas in a diesel: don't start it. The tank needs to be drained
result.now: Don't start the engine. Tell the station staff, then have the vehicle towed to a shop that can drain the tank, ideally one that works on diesels.
if: If you only added a little before you noticed, still don't start it. Let the shop decide whether draining is needed.
Keep your receipt. It shows what was pumped and how much.
result.why: Diesel fuel also oils the high-pressure fuel pump. Gasoline thins it out and can make the pump wear quickly, and on modern diesels a damaged pump can send metal bits through the whole fuel system, which is a much bigger repair. If the engine hasn't run, draining the tank usually prevents that.

causes.name: Gasoline in the fuel tank
causes.clues: Your receipt or the pump says gasoline or unleaded.

causes.name: Gasoline already in the fuel lines
causes.clues: The key was turned to ON, which can run the fuel pump for a moment.

you: Check your receipt for the fuel type and amount.
shop: Drain the fuel tank
Flush the fuel lines and replace the fuel filter
Refill with diesel

result.title: Gas in a diesel after starting: turn it off and have it towed
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn off the engine and don't restart it. Have the vehicle towed to a shop that works on diesels.
if: If the engine knocked, lost power or stalled, tell the shop. The fuel pump and injectors may need to be checked.
If you smell fuel or see a leak, keep away from sparks and flames.
result.why: Running a diesel on gasoline takes away the oiling the fuel pump needs and can cause knocking. The longer it runs, the more likely the pump and injectors are to be damaged. Turning it off quickly limits the damage.

causes.name: Gasoline in the tank and fuel lines
causes.clues: The engine knocked, lost power or ran rough after filling up.

causes.name: Injector damage
causes.clues: Rough running or smoke that doesn't go away.

you: Keep your receipt and note how far the vehicle went after filling up.
shop: Drain the tank and flush the fuel lines
Replace the fuel filter
Check the high-pressure fuel pump and injectors
Code scan

result.title: Lower octane than your car calls for is usually not an emergency
result.now: Go easy on the gas: avoid hard acceleration, towing and heavy loads until you've used most of the tank. Then fill up with the grade your owner's manual or fuel door lists.
if: If the engine knocks, pings or rattles when you speed up, ease off the gas. If it keeps knocking, stop driving and have it checked.
If the check engine light comes on, have the code read.
result.why: Many engines that need premium can adjust themselves to protect against knocking when the octane is lower, so you may only notice a little less power or worse mileage. Hard acceleration and heavy loads make knocking more likely. Your owner's manual says whether premium is required or only recommended.

causes.name: Engine adjusting for lower octane
causes.clues: A little less power or slightly worse mileage.

causes.name: Knocking from low octane
causes.clues: A pinging or rattling sound when you speed up or climb hills.

you: Check your owner's manual for whether premium is required or recommended.
Listen for pinging when you speed up.
shop: Code scan if a warning light comes on
Knock sensor check if pinging continues

result.title: Premium in a car that takes regular won't hurt it
result.now: Nothing needs to be done for the engine. Next time, use the grade your owner's manual lists.
if: If you notice a warning light or the car runs badly, the premium fuel isn't the cause. Use the guide that matches what you're seeing.
result.why: Higher octane fuel only resists knocking. An engine built for regular won't gain anything from it, but it won't be harmed either.

causes.name: Higher octane than needed
causes.clues: Your receipt shows premium, or 91 or 93 octane.

causes.name: A separate running problem
causes.clues: If the car runs badly, something else is likely going on.

you: Check your owner's manual for the right grade.
shop: Code scan only if a warning light comes on

result.title: E85 in a car that isn't built for it can make it run poorly
result.now: Check your fuel door, gas cap and owner's manual for 'E85' or 'Flex Fuel'. If your car isn't flex-fuel, don't run the tank down. Ask a shop within the next few days whether to drain it or mix it with regular gasoline, based on how much E85 went in.
if: If your car turns out to be flex-fuel, E85 is fine and nothing needs to be done.
If the engine stumbles, stalls or the check engine light flashes, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and have it checked.
result.why: E85 has much more alcohol than regular gas. A car that isn't built for it can run lean, hesitate, stall or turn on the check engine light, and over time the alcohol can harm fuel system parts that aren't made for it. Flex-fuel cars usually say so on the fuel door, gas cap or a badge.

causes.name: E85 mixed in the tank
causes.clues: A check engine light, hesitation or rough running after filling up.

causes.name: The car is actually flex-fuel
causes.clues: A Flex Fuel or E85 badge, or a yellow gas cap or ring.

you: Look for a Flex Fuel or E85 label on the fuel door, gas cap or owner's manual.
Keep your receipt to show how much E85 went in.
shop: Code scan
Fuel ethanol content test
Drain the tank if a lot of E85 went in

result.title: If you're not sure what went in, don't start it until you know
result.now: Don't start the engine yet. Check your receipt and the pump you used. If it was diesel in a gas car or gas in a diesel, have the car towed instead of starting it.
if: If the receipt shows the right fuel type and grade, the fill-up is fine.
If you've already started it and it runs rough, smokes or stalls, turn the engine off and have it towed.
result.why: Diesel and gasoline mix-ups can cause serious damage once the engine runs, while most octane mix-ups don't. Taking a minute to check the receipt before starting can save a large repair.

causes.name: Wrong type of fuel
causes.clues: The pump handle or receipt says diesel in a gas car, or gas in a diesel.

causes.name: Wrong grade of gasoline
causes.clues: The receipt shows a different octane than your car calls for.
